text: A cross-validation score tells you how good a model is. It does not tell you what to do about it. Learning curves and validation curves do. They show whether you need more data, a more flexible model, or a simpler one.

The idea is to compare the training score with the validation score. If training is high and validation is far below, the model has high variance: it memorizes. If both are low and close together, it has high bias: it is too simple. If both are high and close, you are in good shape.

The learning_curve function retrains the model on growing slices of the training data and scores each one with cross-validation. For an unpruned decision tree on our illustrative churn data, training accuracy is one point zero at every size. Validation climbs from point seven five to point eight three, and it is still rising.
To see it, plot both. Here we loop over two models, the tree and a logistic regression, and draw a dashed training line and a solid validation line for each.

This is the output of the code above. The tree on the left shows a wide gap, and the validation line is still climbing, so more data or a simpler tree would help. On the right, logistic regression is different. Both curves meet near point eight two and go flat. More rows will not help it. Only a different model or better features can.

A validation curve does the same for one hyperparameter. Here it is the tree's max depth. At depth three, train and validation are close, point eight one and point eight, so the tree underfits. At depth eight, validation peaks at point eight four one. By depth twenty, training is a perfect one and validation slips back to point eight three one.

So the diagnosis gives you an action. A big gap: get more data, simplify the model, or regularize. Both low: use a richer model or better features. Flat and close together: extra rows will not help, so change the model.
